Webhooks
Last reviewed 2026-09-30 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can build a receiver that rejects forged and replayed events, say exactly what a signature must cover and why, and tell a duplicate that is an attack from a duplicate that is the sender doing its job.

Before you start. This module is module 2's signature, module 11's duplicate handling and module 13's limits, applied to an endpoint whose whole job is to be posted to by somebody else.
Published lesson 17 of 27Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: ExampleHotels posts an event to ExampleAir when a payment settles, and ExampleAir credits the account. Company names are fictional.

The endpoint is a public URL that changes your data. It has no session, no token from a login, and no user. Being on the internet authenticates nobody, so the signature is not an extra layer here: it is the entire authentication, and everything about its strength is decided by what it covers.

Which means the interesting failures are not "no signature". They are signatures that verify correctly on a request you should have refused.

Somebody postsNo verificationSignature over the bodyBody and timestamp, window, id recorded
A real event from the senderAppliedAppliedApplied
An invented eventAppliedRefusedRefused
A real event with the amount changedAppliedRefusedRefused
A captured event, replayed a year laterAppliedAppliedRefused
A captured event, replayed within the windowAppliedAppliedApplied once
Two copies arriving before either finishesApplied twiceApplied twiceApplied once
A refund before the payment it refundsApplied in that orderApplied in that orderApplied in that order

The last row never turns green, and it is not a security failure. Delivery is at least once and in no particular order, and a receiver that assumes otherwise is wrong about the protocol rather than about the attacker.
2. Why it works
There is a standard for this, and it is worth knowing

Most webhook implementations follow a vendor's convention. There is also an IETF answer, and it is specific: RFC 8417 defines a Security Event Token, a JWT describing "statements of fact from the perspective of an issuer about a subject", and RFC 8935 defines delivering one over HTTP POST. If you are designing a sender, these are worth reading before inventing a header.

RFC 8935 section 2 lists what a recipient verifies, and the list is a good checklist whatever format you use: that it can parse the event, that the event "is authentic (i.e., it was issued by the issuer specified within the SET)", that the recipient "is identified as an intended audience", that the issuer "is recognized as an issuer that the SET Recipient is willing to receive SETs from", and that the recipient "is willing to accept this SET from this SET Transmitter". Note that the last two are separate questions: who wrote the event and who handed it to you are different, and both need an answer.

RFC 8417 section 2.2 requires iss, iat and jti, defines events, and recommends aud. The jti is the one this module leans on: the specification notes it "MAY be used by clients to track whether a particular SET has already been received", which is module 11's idempotency key arriving under a different name.
What the signature covers is the whole question

A signature over the request body proves the body came from a key holder. It does not say when, so a body captured once is valid forever. Adding a timestamp to the request does nothing on its own, because the attacker sends the timestamp too. The timestamp has to be inside the signed data.

Once it is, the attacker has no move, and it is worth seeing both halves of that. Replay the original timestamp and the event is too old. Substitute a fresh timestamp and the signature no longer verifies, because the timestamp is part of what was signed. The lab shows the first; the second falls out of the same change.

Then the window has to actually be compared against the clock, which is a separate line of code from covering the timestamp, and skipping it leaves you exactly where you started.
Duplicates are normal

This is the part that gets designed wrong most often, because the instinct is to treat a repeated event as an attack. Delivery is at least once. A sender that does not receive your acknowledgement will send again, and it is right to. RFC 8935 section 2 is explicit about how to respond: when an event has already been received, "the SET Recipient MUST respond as it would if the SET had not been previously received".

That requirement does two things. It keeps honest senders from retrying forever, and it stops the response becoming an oracle: a receiver that answers differently for events it has seen has told a prober which event identifiers are real.

So record the identifier, apply the event once, and answer the same way both times. And record it before doing the work, not after, for the reason module 11 gave: two copies arriving close together both find nothing recorded, and both apply.
The whole system
LimitsAuthenticationDeduplicationNot settled
3. The control

1. Apply size limits and a timeout first, then parse under module 13's rules. This is an unauthenticated endpoint until the signature verifies, so the parsing happens before you know who is calling.
  2. Verify a signature over the body and the timestamp together. One value, both inputs. A signature over the body alone is valid forever.
  3. Compare that timestamp against your clock and refuse anything outside a stated window.
  4. Compare in constant time, with a library function built for it.
  5. Claim the event identifier before doing the work, in a store every instance shares.
  6. Answer identically whether or not you have seen the event. RFC 8935 requires it, and it also keeps the endpoint from being a lookup service for event identifiers.
  7. Acknowledge fast and process asynchronously. A sender waiting on your business logic will time out and retry, which produces duplicates you then have to handle anyway.
  8. Do not trust order. Make each handler tolerate arriving first, and reconcile against the sender's state rather than assuming a sequence.
  9. Treat the event as data. Any URL inside it is a caller-supplied URL, which is module 14.
4. Defaults and when to change them

DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
FormatA signed JWT, per RFC 8417, delivered per RFC 8935 if you are designing the senderYou are the receiver and the sender has already chosen. Then implement theirs and apply everything below to it.
What is signedThe timestamp and the raw body, as one valueNever the body alone. Never a re-serialised body: sign and verify the exact bytes.
Freshness window300 seconds, stated in your documentationTighten where clocks are reliable. The window is the replay window for anything you fail to record.
Event identifiersRecorded before processing, in a shared store, kept longer than the windowNever per instance, and never recorded after the work.
The response202 on success, the same for a duplicate, 400 on a bad eventRFC 8935 specifies 202 for a valid event and 400 for one that fails parsing, validation or authentication, and requires the duplicate to look like the first.
ProcessingAcknowledge first, work asynchronouslySynchronous processing turns your slow day into the sender's retry storm.
OrderingAssume noneReconcile against the sender's current state where order genuinely matters.
SecretsOne per sender, rotatable with an overlapA shared secret across senders means any of them can forge as another. Module 3 applies here too.
Endpoint URLNot a secretAn unguessable URL is not authentication. It leaks in logs, referrers and support tickets.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: that a key holder produced this exact body recently, and that you have applied it once.

Doesn't prove: that it arrived in order, that it is the only event in flight, or that the sender is who the body says they are rather than whoever holds the key. It also says nothing about the contents: a correctly signed event carrying a URL you fetch is module 14's problem, arriving with a valid signature.

A duplicate is usually your sender doing the right thing. The instinct to treat a repeated event as hostile produces receivers that answer differently the second time, which breaks honest retries and tells a prober which identifiers exist. Record the identifier, apply once, answer the same way, and the honest case and the hostile case become the same code path.
6. Prove it

For each webhook endpoint:

  • An unsigned post is refused.
  • A post signed with another sender's secret is refused.
  • A valid body with one byte changed is refused.
  • A captured event replayed outside the window is refused, and the test shows which check refused it.
  • A captured event replayed with a fresh timestamp is refused, which proves the timestamp is covered.
  • The same event delivered twice is applied once, with identical responses.
  • Two copies delivered concurrently are applied once, tested against two instances.
  • A large or deeply nested body is refused before parsing completes.
  • Events arriving out of order leave correct state, or the design says why they cannot.
  • All of the above are tests in the build.
Download labs/webhook_lab.py. It needs nothing beyond Python 3.

Windows              macOS and Linux
py -3 labs/webhook_lab.py    python3 labs/webhook_lab.py

There is no python3 command on a default Windows install, so use py -3 there. Every signature is a real HMAC over the real bytes. The transport is a stub, so nothing listens on a port. The keys are random per run and no key material is printed, so the output is the same every time.

$ python3 labs/webhook_lab.py
key source: random, this run only; no secret is printed

Part A: a receiver that verifies nothing.
 1. the real sender posts an event                       202 accepted
 2. anyone who knows the URL posts one                   202 accepted
 3. events applied                                       2

Part B: a signature over the body and the timestamp.
 4. the real sender, correctly signed                    202 accepted
 5. an unsigned post                                     400 no signature
 6. signed with the wrong key                            400 signature check failed
 7. the body altered after signing                       400 signature check failed
 8. events applied                                       1

Part C: the four details.
 9. signature over the body alone, replayed a year later 202 accepted
10. the same replay, timestamp covered and checked       400 event too old
11. timestamp covered but never compared to the clock    202 accepted
12. the same event twice, ids not recorded               2 applied
13. the same event twice, ids recorded                   202 accepted
14.   and applied only once                              1 applied
15. id recorded after processing, two copies interleaved 2 applied
16.   the same interleaving, id claimed first            202 accepted
17.   events applied                                     1 applied

Part D: what the signature does not settle.
18. a legitimate retry from the sender                   202 accepted
19.   the response differs from the first                False
20.   and it was applied once                            1 applied
21. a refund applied before the payment it refunds       ['payment.refunded', 'payment.settled']
22. a prober posts a known id with no signature          400 no signature

all lab checks passed

Check 9 is the one worth sitting with. The signature covers the body and nothing else, so the attacker replays a year-old event and supplies a fresh timestamp of their own, and the freshness check has nothing to object to. The timestamp was present in the request the whole time and it was never evidence of anything, because the attacker wrote it.

Check 10 is the fix, and it closes both moves at once. Keep the original timestamp and the event is too old. Substitute a fresh one and the signature stops verifying, because the timestamp is part of what was signed. Check 11 is the reminder that covering it and comparing it are two separate lines of code.

Checks 15 to 17 are two copies of one event interleaved explicitly: both verify before either finishes. With the identifier claimed after the work, both apply. With it claimed first, the second copy is acknowledged with the same 202 and not applied, and the event happens once.

Checks 18 to 20 are the case that is not an attack at all. A sender that did not get your acknowledgement retries, which is correct behaviour, and your receiver answers identically and applies nothing. Check 19 is the requirement RFC 8935 states, tested.

Try next:

  • Set cover_timestamp=False on the Part B receiver and rerun. The run exits 1 with two changes: check 4 prints 400 signature check failed and check 8 counts 0, because the sender still signs the timestamp and the receiver no longer does. The two sides have to agree on what is covered. Then reread check 9.
  • Replace hmac.compare_digest with == and rerun. Every check still passes, which is module 2's point in a new place.
  • Add a third event that depends on the first two and make the handler assume order. Then run them in the order check 21 produces.
  • Make the receiver return 409 for an event it has already applied and rerun. The run exits 1 with four changes: checks 13, 16 and 18 print 409 conflict and check 19 prints True. Check 22 does not change, because an unsigned post is refused before the identifier is looked up. Then write down what somebody replaying a captured, correctly signed event learns from the 409.
8. Check your understanding

Your webhook signature covers the request body. What can an attacker who captured one event do?

Replay it, indefinitely. The signature is valid for as long as the secret is, and the body does not change. Adding a timestamp to the request does not help on its own, because the attacker supplies that too. The timestamp has to be inside the signed value, and then compared against your clock.

Why must a receiver answer the same way for an event it has already applied?

RFC 8935 requires it, and for two good reasons. An honest sender that did not get your acknowledgement will keep retrying until it does, and a receiver that answers differently the second time has told anybody who asks which event identifiers exist.

Your endpoint URL is a long random string. How much authentication is that?

None. A URL travels in logs, proxies, browser history, support tickets and configuration files, and it is sent on every delivery. Treat it as public and let the signature do the authenticating.

A refund event arrives before the payment it refunds. Whose bug is that?

Nobody's, in most systems. Delivery is at least once and unordered, so a receiver that assumes a sequence has assumed something the protocol never offered. Make each handler tolerate arriving first, or reconcile against the sender's current state where order genuinely matters.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. The attacker controls every value they send, including the timestamp, so freshness only means something when the timestamp is inside the signed value.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. The five-minute window, constant-time comparison and a secret URL are all worth having, and none of them stops a captured event being replayed with a timestamp the attacker chose.

blocks.html:
Quick check

Replay

Your receiver checks an HMAC over the request body and refuses events whose timestamp field is more than five minutes old. What stops a captured event being replayed?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/webhook_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant. One edit changes nothing the lab prints, and its answer carries the measurement from a request the lab does not make.

1. The replay in check 10 carries a fresh timestamp

Check 10 replays a year-old event with its original timestamp. In main, make the attacker send a fresh timestamp with the old signature instead, as check 9 does. The receiver stays as it is:

covered.post(body, sign(secret, body, NOW),
             timestamp=NOW + 31536000, now=NOW + 31536000)
What does check 10 print?

Every option, and why
  • The window test compares the timestamp that was sent with the clock, and both are now NOW + 31536000, so by that test the event is fresh. The request never gets that far, because the signature is compared first.
  • Check 9 prints 202 accepted because its receiver is built with cover_timestamp=False and verifies the body alone. This receiver recomputes the signature over the timestamp it was sent and the body.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 10 goes from 400 event too old to 400 signature check failed. The signature was made over the original timestamp, the receiver recomputes it over the fresh one, and the two values differ. Section 2 says this second move "falls out of the same change", and this is it, measured. The exit code only means the lab expected the other refusal. Check hook-01 in the Reference layer asks for both replays as tests, refused for different reasons, and the published lab runs only the first.
  • Nothing raises. A disagreement between the timestamp and the signature is exactly what the comparison is there to find, and it answers with a response, not an exception.

2. The timestamp is never compared with the clock

In Receiver.reserve, delete the two lines that return 400 event too old. The signature still covers the timestamp.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 10 goes from 400 event too old to 202 accepted, which is what check 11 already prints for a receiver built with check_window=False. Covering the timestamp stops the attacker changing it. It does not make anybody read it. With the comparison gone, a captured event stays valid for as long as the secret does. Check hook-02 in the Reference layer is this one comparison, and its test is an event outside the window.
  • That is the answer when the attacker changes the timestamp. Here the replay carries the original timestamp and the original signature, and those still match.
  • Check 11 prints 202 accepted before and after. Its receiver never compared the timestamp, and this edit makes every receiver behave like it.
  • The year-old event verifies perfectly. The signature was made over that timestamp and that body, and the replay sends both unchanged. A covered timestamp shows the value was not altered, not that it is recent.

3. The identifier is recorded after the work by default

In Receiver.__init__, change the default record_before=True to record_before=False. A receiver built without that argument now records the identifier in apply, after it has processed the event.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 14 posts the two copies one after the other. The first post finishes, and records the identifier, before the second begins, so the second is still answered without being applied.
  • The receiver behind checks 16 and 17 is built with record_before=True passed explicitly, so the default never reaches it.
  • The retry in Part D is also two posts in sequence. The first has recorded the identifier by the time the retry arrives, so check 20 still prints 1 applied.
  • Correct. Exit 0, 33 of 33 lines identical. Every receiver that relies on the default handles its copies one at a time, and the two receivers that interleave pass record_before explicitly. Measured with a request the lab does not make, the interleaving of checks 15 to 17 against a receiver built with the defaults: as published the second copy is answered 202 accepted and the count is 1 applied, and with the edit both copies are processed and the count is 2 applied. A test suite that only sends duplicates in sequence passes on both versions. Check hook-03 in the Reference layer asks for two concurrent copies, not two sequential requests, for this reason.

4. The identifier is looked up before the signature is verified

In Receiver.reserve, move the whole if self.record_ids: block above the if self.verify: block, so an event the receiver has already seen is answered without any signature work. Nothing else changes.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 7 changes too. The altered body keeps the identifier evt-1001, which check 4 already recorded, so the receiver answers before it reads the signature.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: check 7 goes from 400 signature check failed to 202 accepted, and check 22 from 400 no signature to 202 accepted. Neither event is applied, and check 8 still prints 1. The damage is in the responses. An unsigned post now gets 202 accepted for an identifier the receiver has seen and 400 no signature for one it has not, so anybody can sort identifiers into the two groups without the secret. Measured with a request the lab does not make, an unsigned post naming evt-2001, which the receiver has not seen, followed by the real, correctly signed event with that identifier: as published the answers are 400 no signature then 202 accepted, and the count is 1 applied. With the edit the answers are the same and the count is 0 applied, because the unsigned post claimed the identifier before it was refused. Check hook-04 in the Reference layer says a different response reveals which identifiers exist, and this edit hands that difference to callers who never verified.
  • Check 8 still prints 1. The duplicate branch returns before apply runs, so the altered amount is acknowledged and never applied.
  • The order decides which answer an unverified caller gets. As published, a caller without a valid signature never reaches the identifier store, so it can neither read from it nor write to it.

Reference
Controls
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

• StandardA Security Event Token is a JWT describing "statements of fact from the perspective of an issuer about a subject", with iss, iat and jti REQUIRED, events carrying the event statements, and aud RECOMMENDED. RFC 8417 sections 1 and 2.2.
  • StandardThe jti is REQUIRED and "MUST be unique within a particular event feed", and it "MAY be used by clients to track whether a particular SET has already been received". RFC 8417 section 2.2.
  • StandardVerify that you can parse the event, that it "is authentic (i.e., it was issued by the issuer specified within the SET)", that you are "identified as an intended audience", that the issuer is one you are "willing to receive SETs from", and that you are "willing to accept this SET from this SET Transmitter". RFC 8935 section 2. Who wrote it and who delivered it are separate questions.
  • StandardAcknowledge a valid event with 202 Accepted, and respond to an error with 400 Bad Request. RFC 8935 sections 2.2 and 2.3.
  • StandardFor an event already received, "the SET Recipient MUST respond as it would if the SET had not been previously received". RFC 8935 section 2.
  • StandardSecurity events carrying personal data or passing through third parties "MUST be encrypted using JWE or secured for confidentiality by other means", and integrity requires signing unless ensured by other means. RFC 8417 section 5.1.
  • StandardWhere the sender signs HTTP requests rather than the payload, use RFC 9421 and cover a body digest, as in module 3.
  • BaselineSign the timestamp and the raw body as one value, and verify the exact bytes received rather than a re-serialised form.
  • BaselineCompare the covered timestamp against your clock, with a stated window of 300 seconds.
  • BaselineCompare signatures in constant time.
  • BaselineClaim the event identifier before processing, in a store every instance shares, and keep it longer than the freshness window.
  • BaselineAcknowledge first and process asynchronously, so a slow handler does not become a retry storm.
  • BaselineUse one secret per sender, rotatable with an overlap. A shared secret lets any sender forge as another.
  • BaselineTreat the endpoint URL as public and the event contents as untrusted input, including any URL inside them.
  • OptionHave the sender authenticate the connection as well, with mutual TLS, which RFC 8935 section 3 names as one way to establish the transmitter's identity.
  • OptionReconcile periodically against the sender's API rather than relying on delivery alone, which covers both lost events and ordering.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• The signature covers the timestamp as well as the body Test a replay with the original timestamp and a replay with a fresh one. Both must be refused, for different reasons.
  • The covered timestamp is compared against a clock Covering it and checking it are two separate lines. Test an event outside the window.
  • Event identifiers are claimed before processing, in a shared store Test two concurrent copies against two instances, not two sequential requests.
  • A duplicate gets the same response as the original RFC 8935 requires it. A different response breaks honest retries and reveals which identifiers exist.
  • Size limits and parsing limits apply before the signature check The endpoint is unauthenticated until the signature verifies, so the parser meets attacker input first.
  • One secret per sender, rotatable with an overlap A shared secret lets any sender forge as another.
  • Handlers tolerate out-of-order delivery Or the design states why order is guaranteed. Delivery is at least once and unordered.
  • The endpoint URL is not treated as a secret And the event contents are treated as untrusted input, including any URL inside them.
Sources

• RFC 8417: Security Event Token (SET), July 2018. Sections 1, 2.2 and 5.1.
  • RFC 8935: Push-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Using HTTP, November 2020. Sections 2, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and 3.
  • RFC 9421: HTTP Message Signatures, February 2024. For senders signing the request rather than the payload.

Record the identifier, apply once, answer the same way, and the honest case and the hostile case become the same code path.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
For each webhook endpoint:

  • An unsigned post is refused.
  • A post signed with another sender's secret is refused.
  • A valid body with one byte changed is refused.
  • A captured event replayed outside the window is refused, and the test shows which check refused it.
  • A captured event replayed with a fresh timestamp is refused, which proves the timestamp is covered.
  • The same event delivered twice is applied once, with identical responses.
  • Two copies delivered concurrently are applied once, tested against two instances.
  • A large or deeply nested body is refused before parsing completes.
  • Events arriving out of order leave correct state, or the design says why they cannot.
  • All of the above are tests in the build.

sections.heading: 7. Lab
sections.html:
Download labs/webhook_lab.py. It needs nothing beyond Python 3.

Windows              macOS and Linux
py -3 labs/webhook_lab.py    python3 labs/webhook_lab.py

There is no python3 command on a default Windows install, so use py -3 there. Every signature is a real HMAC over the real bytes. The transport is a stub, so nothing listens on a port. The keys are random per run and no key material is printed, so the output is the same every time.

$ python3 labs/webhook_lab.py
key source: random, this run only; no secret is printed

Part A: a receiver that verifies nothing.
 1. the real sender posts an event                       202 accepted
 2. anyone who knows the URL posts one                   202 accepted
 3. events applied                                       2

Part B: a signature over the body and the timestamp.
 4. the real sender, correctly signed                    202 accepted
 5. an unsigned post                                     400 no signature
 6. signed with the wrong key                            400 signature check failed
 7. the body altered after signing                       400 signature check failed
 8. events applied                                       1

Part C: the four details.
 9. signature over the body alone, replayed a year later 202 accepted
10. the same replay, timestamp covered and checked       400 event too old
11. timestamp covered but never compared to the clock    202 accepted
12. the same event twice, ids not recorded               2 applied
13. the same event twice, ids recorded                   202 accepted
14.   and applied only once                              1 applied
15. id recorded after processing, two copies interleaved 2 applied
16.   the same interleaving, id claimed first            202 accepted
17.   events applied                                     1 applied

Part D: what the signature does not settle.
18. a legitimate retry from the sender                   202 accepted
19.   the response differs from the first                False
20.   and it was applied once                            1 applied
21. a refund applied before the payment it refunds       ['payment.refunded', 'payment.settled']
22. a prober posts a known id with no signature          400 no signature

all lab checks passed

Check 9 is the one worth sitting with. The signature covers the body and nothing else, so the attacker replays a year-old event and supplies a fresh timestamp of their own, and the freshness check has nothing to object to. The timestamp was present in the request the whole time and it was never evidence of anything, because the attacker wrote it.

Check 10 is the fix, and it closes both moves at once. Keep the original timestamp and the event is too old. Substitute a fresh one and the signature stops verifying, because the timestamp is part of what was signed. Check 11 is the reminder that covering it and comparing it are two separate lines of code.

Checks 15 to 17 are two copies of one event interleaved explicitly: both verify before either finishes. With the identifier claimed after the work, both apply. With it claimed first, the second copy is acknowledged with the same 202 and not applied, and the event happens once.

Checks 18 to 20 are the case that is not an attack at all. A sender that did not get your acknowledgement retries, which is correct behaviour, and your receiver answers identically and applies nothing. Check 19 is the requirement RFC 8935 states, tested.

Try next:

  • Set cover_timestamp=False on the Part B receiver and rerun. The run exits 1 with two changes: check 4 prints 400 signature check failed and check 8 counts 0, because the sender still signs the timestamp and the receiver no longer does. The two sides have to agree on what is covered. Then reread check 9.
  • Replace hmac.compare_digest with == and rerun. Every check still passes, which is module 2's point in a new place.
  • Add a third event that depends on the first two and make the handler assume order. Then run them in the order check 21 produces.
  • Make the receiver return 409 for an event it has already applied and rerun. The run exits 1 with four changes: checks 13, 16 and 18 print 409 conflict and check 19 prints True. Check 22 does not change, because an unsigned post is refused before the identifier is looked up. Then write down what somebody replaying a captured, correctly signed event learns from the 409.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
Your webhook signature covers the request body. What can an attacker who captured one event do?

Replay it, indefinitely. The signature is valid for as long as the secret is, and the body does not change. Adding a timestamp to the request does not help on its own, because the attacker supplies that too. The timestamp has to be inside the signed value, and then compared against your clock.

Why must a receiver answer the same way for an event it has already applied?

RFC 8935 requires it, and for two good reasons. An honest sender that did not get your acknowledgement will keep retrying until it does, and a receiver that answers differently the second time has told anybody who asks which event identifiers exist.

Your endpoint URL is a long random string. How much authentication is that?

None. A URL travels in logs, proxies, browser history, support tickets and configuration files, and it is sent on every delivery. Treat it as public and let the signature do the authenticating.

A refund event arrives before the payment it refunds. Whose bug is that?

Nobody's, in most systems. Delivery is at least once and unordered, so a receiver that assumes a sequence has assumed something the protocol never offered. Make each handler tolerate arriving first, or reconcile against the sender's current state where order genuinely matters.

Quick check

sections.heading: Replay
sections.html:
Your receiver checks an HMAC over the request body and refuses events whose timestamp field is more than five minutes old. What stops a captured event being replayed?

Exercises

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/webhook_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant. One edit changes nothing the lab prints, and its answer carries the measurement from a request the lab does not make.

1. The replay in check 10 carries a fresh timestamp

Check 10 replays a year-old event with its original timestamp. In main, make the attacker send a fresh timestamp with the old signature instead, as check 9 does. The receiver stays as it is:

covered.post(body, sign(secret, body, NOW),
             timestamp=NOW + 31536000, now=NOW + 31536000)
What does check 10 print?

Every option, and why
  • The window test compares the timestamp that was sent with the clock, and both are now NOW + 31536000, so by that test the event is fresh. The request never gets that far, because the signature is compared first.
  • Check 9 prints 202 accepted because its receiver is built with cover_timestamp=False and verifies the body alone. This receiver recomputes the signature over the timestamp it was sent and the body.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 10 goes from 400 event too old to 400 signature check failed. The signature was made over the original timestamp, the receiver recomputes it over the fresh one, and the two values differ. Section 2 says this second move "falls out of the same change", and this is it, measured. The exit code only means the lab expected the other refusal. Check hook-01 in the Reference layer asks for both replays as tests, refused for different reasons, and the published lab runs only the first.
  • Nothing raises. A disagreement between the timestamp and the signature is exactly what the comparison is there to find, and it answers with a response, not an exception.

2. The timestamp is never compared with the clock

In Receiver.reserve, delete the two lines that return 400 event too old. The signature still covers the timestamp.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 10 goes from 400 event too old to 202 accepted, which is what check 11 already prints for a receiver built with check_window=False. Covering the timestamp stops the attacker changing it. It does not make anybody read it. With the comparison gone, a captured event stays valid for as long as the secret does. Check hook-02 in the Reference layer is this one comparison, and its test is an event outside the window.
  • That is the answer when the attacker changes the timestamp. Here the replay carries the original timestamp and the original signature, and those still match.
  • Check 11 prints 202 accepted before and after. Its receiver never compared the timestamp, and this edit makes every receiver behave like it.
  • The year-old event verifies perfectly. The signature was made over that timestamp and that body, and the replay sends both unchanged. A covered timestamp shows the value was not altered, not that it is recent.

3. The identifier is recorded after the work by default

In Receiver.__init__, change the default record_before=True to record_before=False. A receiver built without that argument now records the identifier in apply, after it has processed the event.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 14 posts the two copies one after the other. The first post finishes, and records the identifier, before the second begins, so the second is still answered without being applied.
  • The receiver behind checks 16 and 17 is built with record_before=True passed explicitly, so the default never reaches it.
  • The retry in Part D is also two posts in sequence. The first has recorded the identifier by the time the retry arrives, so check 20 still prints 1 applied.
  • Correct. Exit 0, 33 of 33 lines identical. Every receiver that relies on the default handles its copies one at a time, and the two receivers that interleave pass record_before explicitly. Measured with a request the lab does not make, the interleaving of checks 15 to 17 against a receiver built with the defaults: as published the second copy is answered 202 accepted and the count is 1 applied, and with the edit both copies are processed and the count is 2 applied. A test suite that only sends duplicates in sequence passes on both versions. Check hook-03 in the Reference layer asks for two concurrent copies, not two sequential requests, for this reason.

4. The identifier is looked up before the signature is verified

In Receiver.reserve, move the whole if self.record_ids: block above the if self.verify: block, so an event the receiver has already seen is answered without any signature work. Nothing else changes.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 7 changes too. The altered body keeps the identifier evt-1001, which check 4 already recorded, so the receiver answers before it reads the signature.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: check 7 goes from 400 signature check failed to 202 accepted, and check 22 from 400 no signature to 202 accepted. Neither event is applied, and check 8 still prints 1. The damage is in the responses. An unsigned post now gets 202 accepted for an identifier the receiver has seen and 400 no signature for one it has not, so anybody can sort identifiers into the two groups without the secret. Measured with a request the lab does not make, an unsigned post naming evt-2001, which the receiver has not seen, followed by the real, correctly signed event with that identifier: as published the answers are 400 no signature then 202 accepted, and the count is 1 applied. With the edit the answers are the same and the count is 0 applied, because the unsigned post claimed the identifier before it was refused. Check hook-04 in the Reference layer says a different response reveals which identifiers exist, and this edit hands that difference to callers who never verified.
  • Check 8 still prints 1. The duplicate branch returns before apply runs, so the altered amount is acknowledged and never applied.
  • The order decides which answer an unverified caller gets. As published, a caller without a valid signature never reaches the identifier store, so it can neither read from it nor write to it.

Course progress: return to the course dashboard to see your published-module progress.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardA Security Event Token is a JWT describing "statements of fact from the perspective of an issuer about a subject", with iss, iat and jti REQUIRED, events carrying the event statements, and aud RECOMMENDED. RFC 8417 sections 1 and 2.2.
  • StandardThe jti is REQUIRED and "MUST be unique within a particular event feed", and it "MAY be used by clients to track whether a particular SET has already been received". RFC 8417 section 2.2.
  • StandardVerify that you can parse the event, that it "is authentic (i.e., it was issued by the issuer specified within the SET)", that you are "identified as an intended audience", that the issuer is one you are "willing to receive SETs from", and that you are "willing to accept this SET from this SET Transmitter". RFC 8935 section 2. Who wrote it and who delivered it are separate questions.
  • StandardAcknowledge a valid event with 202 Accepted, and respond to an error with 400 Bad Request. RFC 8935 sections 2.2 and 2.3.
  • StandardFor an event already received, "the SET Recipient MUST respond as it would if the SET had not been previously received". RFC 8935 section 2.
  • StandardSecurity events carrying personal data or passing through third parties "MUST be encrypted using JWE or secured for confidentiality by other means", and integrity requires signing unless ensured by other means. RFC 8417 section 5.1.
  • StandardWhere the sender signs HTTP requests rather than the payload, use RFC 9421 and cover a body digest, as in module 3.
  • BaselineSign the timestamp and the raw body as one value, and verify the exact bytes received rather than a re-serialised form.
  • BaselineCompare the covered timestamp against your clock, with a stated window of 300 seconds.
  • BaselineCompare signatures in constant time.
  • BaselineClaim the event identifier before processing, in a store every instance shares, and keep it longer than the freshness window.
  • BaselineAcknowledge first and process asynchronously, so a slow handler does not become a retry storm.
  • BaselineUse one secret per sender, rotatable with an overlap. A shared secret lets any sender forge as another.
  • BaselineTreat the endpoint URL as public and the event contents as untrusted input, including any URL inside them.
  • OptionHave the sender authenticate the connection as well, with mutual TLS, which RFC 8935 section 3 names as one way to establish the transmitter's identity.
  • OptionReconcile periodically against the sender's API rather than relying on delivery alone, which covers both lost events and ordering.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • The signature covers the timestamp as well as the body Test a replay with the original timestamp and a replay with a fresh one. Both must be refused, for different reasons.
  • The covered timestamp is compared against a clock Covering it and checking it are two separate lines. Test an event outside the window.
  • Event identifiers are claimed before processing, in a shared store Test two concurrent copies against two instances, not two sequential requests.
  • A duplicate gets the same response as the original RFC 8935 requires it. A different response breaks honest retries and reveals which identifiers exist.
  • Size limits and parsing limits apply before the signature check The endpoint is unauthenticated until the signature verifies, so the parser meets attacker input first.
  • One secret per sender, rotatable with an overlap A shared secret lets any sender forge as another.
  • Handlers tolerate out-of-order delivery Or the design states why order is guaranteed. Delivery is at least once and unordered.
  • The endpoint URL is not treated as a secret And the event contents are treated as untrusted input, including any URL inside them.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.html:
• RFC 8417: Security Event Token (SET), July 2018. Sections 1, 2.2 and 5.1.
  • RFC 8935: Push-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Using HTTP, November 2020. Sections 2, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and 3.
  • RFC 9421: HTTP Message Signatures, February 2024. For senders signing the request rather than the payload.

Measured with a request the lab does not make, an unsigned post naming evt-2001, which the receiver has not seen, followed by the real, correctly signed event with that identifier: as published the answers are 400 no signature then 202 accepted, and the count is 1 applied.   • The order decides which answer an unverified caller gets. As published, a caller without a valid signature never reaches the identifier store, so it can neither read from it nor write to it.

quiz.summary: Your webhook signature covers the request body. What can an attacker who captured one event do?
quiz.html:
Your webhook signature covers the request body. What can an attacker who captured one event do?

Replay it, indefinitely. The signature is valid for as long as the secret is, and the body does not change. Adding a timestamp to the request does not help on its own, because the attacker supplies that too. The timestamp has to be inside the signed value, and then compared against your clock.

quiz.summary: Why must a receiver answer the same way for an event it has already applied?
quiz.html:
Why must a receiver answer the same way for an event it has already applied?

RFC 8935 requires it, and for two good reasons. An honest sender that did not get your acknowledgement will keep retrying until it does, and a receiver that answers differently the second time has told anybody who asks which event identifiers exist.

quiz.summary: Your endpoint URL is a long random string. How much authentication is that?
quiz.html:
Your endpoint URL is a long random string. How much authentication is that?

None. A URL travels in logs, proxies, browser history, support tickets and configuration files, and it is sent on every delivery. Treat it as public and let the signature do the authenticating.

quiz.summary: A refund event arrives before the payment it refunds. Whose bug is that?
quiz.html:
A refund event arrives before the payment it refunds. Whose bug is that?

Nobody's, in most systems. Delivery is at least once and unordered, so a receiver that assumes a sequence has assumed something the protocol never offered. Make each handler tolerate arriving first, or reconcile against the sender's current state where order genuinely matters.

exercises.heading: 1. The replay in check 10 carries a fresh timestamp
exercises.heading_text: 1. The replay in check 10 carries a fresh timestamp

options.label: A traceback, because the timestamp and the signature no longer agree.

answers.html: The window test compares the timestamp that was sent with the clock, and both are now NOW + 31536000, so by that test the event is fresh. The request never gets that far, because the signature is compared first.
Check 9 prints 202 accepted because its receiver is built with cover_timestamp=False and verifies the body alone. This receiver recomputes the signature over the timestamp it was sent and the body.

Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 10 goes from 400 event too old to 400 signature check failed. The signature was made over the original timestamp, the receiver recomputes it over the fresh one, and the two values differ. Section 2 says this second move "falls out of the same change", and this is it, measured. The exit code only means the lab expected the other refusal. Check hook-01 in the Reference layer asks for both replays as tests, refused for different reasons, and the published lab runs only the first.
Nothing raises. A disagreement between the timestamp and the signature is exactly what the comparison is there to find, and it answers with a response, not an exception.

exercises.heading: 2. The timestamp is never compared with the clock
exercises.heading_text: 2. The timestamp is never compared with the clock
exercises.legend: What does the run print differently?

options.label: Nothing. The signature covers the timestamp, so a year-old event cannot verify.

answers.html: Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 10 goes from 400 event too old to 202 accepted, which is what check 11 already prints for a receiver built with check_window=False. Covering the timestamp stops the attacker changing it. It does not make anybody read it. With the comparison gone, a captured event stays valid for as long as the secret does. Check hook-02 in the Reference layer is this one comparison, and its test is an event outside the window.
That is the answer when the attacker changes the timestamp. Here the replay carries the original timestamp and the original signature, and those still match.
Check 11 prints 202 accepted before and after. Its receiver never compared the timestamp, and this edit makes every receiver behave like it.

The year-old event verifies perfectly. The signature was made over that timestamp and that body, and the replay sends both unchanged. A covered timestamp shows the value was not altered, not that it is recent.

exercises.heading: 3. The identifier is recorded after the work by default
exercises.heading_text: 3. The identifier is recorded after the work by default
exercises.legend: What does the run print differently?

options.label: Checks 18 to 20 change, because the retry is applied a second time.

answers.html: Check 14 posts the two copies one after the other. The first post finishes, and records the identifier, before the second begins, so the second is still answered without being applied.
The receiver behind checks 16 and 17 is built with record_before=True passed explicitly, so the default never reaches it.
The retry in Part D is also two posts in sequence. The first has recorded the identifier by the time the retry arrives, so check 20 still prints 1 applied.

Correct. Exit 0, 33 of 33 lines identical. Every receiver that relies on the default handles its copies one at a time, and the two receivers that interleave pass record_before explicitly. Measured with a request the lab does not make, the interleaving of checks 15 to 17 against a receiver built with the defaults: as published the second copy is answered 202 accepted and the count is 1 applied, and with the edit both copies are processed and the count is 2 applied. A test suite that only sends duplicates in sequence passes on both versions. Check hook-03 in the Reference layer asks for two concurrent copies, not two sequential requests, for this reason.
